why_correct: A minus B is the part of A outside B, so the union is that part together with all of B, with no overlap between them. That gives n of A union B equal to 47 plus 326, which is 373.

why_wrong.0: 173 is far too small. The union must be at least as large as B alone, which is already 326.
why_wrong.1: 273 is likewise smaller than B, so it can be ruled out without any calculation.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct option, so none of these does not apply. Note that n of A is not needed at all here, and it is offered to tempt you into adding 115 and 326.

why_correct: Statement 1 is true, since removing B from A removes exactly the elements of A that lie in B. Statement 2 is true, because every element of A either lies in B or does not. Statement 3 is false, so only 1 and 2 hold.

why_wrong.0: This includes statement 3, which is wrong. The correct identity is A minus B union C equals A minus B intersection A minus C, with an intersection rather than a union. This is one of De Morgan's laws for sets.
why_wrong.1: Statement 2 is true, but so is statement 1, so only 2 is too narrow.
why_wrong.2: This again accepts statement 3. Test it with a small example: take A as 1 and 2, B as 1 and C as 2, and the two sides come out different.

why_correct: The domain of a relation is the set of first elements of its ordered pairs. Those first elements here are 1, 2 and 2, so the domain is the set containing 1 and 2.

why_wrong.1: 2 and 3 mixes a first element with a second. 3 appears only as a second element, so it belongs to the range.
why_wrong.2: 1 and 3 makes the same mistake with 3.
why_wrong.3: The whole of A would be the domain only if every element of A appeared as a first element, but 3 never does. The domain is a subset of A, not necessarily all of it.

why_correct: The range is the set of second elements. Those are b, c and c, so the range is the set containing b and c.

why_wrong.0: a and b takes a as a range element, but a appears only in the first position, so it is in the domain.
why_wrong.2: a and c makes the same error with a.
why_wrong.3: All three would require a to appear as a second element somewhere, and it never does. Domain and range are read from opposite sides of the pairs.

why_correct: Since cosec is the reciprocal of sin, a number plus its reciprocal equals 2 only when that number is 1. So sin theta is 1, and 1 to the hundredth plus 1 to the hundredth is 2.

why_wrong.1: 2 to the power 100 would come from raising the whole given expression to the hundredth power, which is not what the question asks.
why_wrong.2: 2 to the power 99 is another version of the same mistake.
why_wrong.3: There is a correct option. The key insight is that x plus 1 over x is at least 2 for positive x, with equality only at x equal to 1, so the condition pins sin theta exactly.

why_correct: If 8 theta is pi then 7 theta is pi minus theta, and cos of pi minus theta is minus cos theta. So the sum is minus cos theta plus cos theta, which is 0.

why_wrong.1: Minus 1 would need the two terms to differ by 1 rather than cancel. They are exact opposites.
why_wrong.2: 1 would need them to be equal and each a half, which they are not.
why_wrong.3: 2 would need both to equal 1, which would require theta to be 0, contradicting 8 theta equal to pi. Using the supplementary identity is quicker than evaluating cos of pi over 8.

why_correct: sin of 180 plus theta is minus sin theta, and sin of 180 minus theta is plus sin theta. Their product is minus sin squared theta, and multiplying by cosec squared theta, which is 1 over sin squared theta, gives minus 1.

why_wrong.0: 0 would need one of the factors to vanish, but none does for general theta.
why_wrong.2: 1 comes from getting both signs positive. Only one of the two shifts changes the sign of sine: adding 180 does, subtracting from 180 does not.
why_wrong.3: There is a definite answer, so none of these is wrong.

why_correct: Multiplying by minus 1 rotates a complex number by half a turn. If the argument of z is negative, lying between minus pi and 0, then adding pi keeps the result within the principal range, so the difference of the arguments is pi.

why_wrong.1: Minus pi would be the answer if the argument of z were positive, since then pi would have to be subtracted to stay in the principal range. That is why the question specifies a negative argument.
why_wrong.2: Pi over 2 is a quarter turn, which corresponds to multiplying by i, not by minus 1.
why_wrong.3: Minus pi over 2 is a quarter turn the other way.

why_correct: The modulus is a distance, so the condition says z is nearer to 4 than to 2. The dividing line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, at 3, and the nearer side to 4 is where the real part exceeds 3.

why_wrong.0: The real part being greater than 0 is far too wide. The point 1, for instance, satisfies it but is nearer to 2 than to 4.
why_wrong.1: The real part being less than 0 is on the wrong side altogether.
why_wrong.3: Greater than 2 includes points between 2 and 3, which are still nearer to 2. The boundary is the midpoint of 2 and 4, which is 3, not 2.

why_correct: The number minus 4 lies on the negative real axis, so its amplitude, measured from the positive real axis, is pi.

why_wrong.0: Pi over 2 is the positive imaginary axis, which would be a purely imaginary number such as 4i.
why_wrong.1: Pi over 3 would need equal-signed real and imaginary parts in a particular ratio, but this number has no imaginary part at all.
why_wrong.3: Pi over 6 likewise requires an imaginary part. Sketching the point on the Argand plane settles this immediately.

why_correct: The sum of the roots is 5, so beta is 5 minus alpha. Putting that into 3 alpha plus 2 beta equal to 12 gives alpha equal to 2, so beta is 3, and K is the product, 6.

why_wrong.0: 5 is the sum of the roots, not their product. The coefficient of x gives the sum and the constant gives the product.
why_wrong.2: 8 would need roots multiplying to 8 and adding to 5, and no such pair satisfies the extra condition.
why_wrong.3: 10 similarly fails. Check any answer by confirming that both the sum condition and the given relation hold.

why_correct: For every real x, x squared is at least 0 and 3 times the modulus of x is at least 0, so the left side is at least 2 and can never be 0. There are no real solutions.

why_wrong.1: 1 would require the expression to touch zero exactly once, but its smallest value is 2, at x equal to 0.
why_wrong.2: 2 is what you would get by treating this as x squared plus 3x plus 2, forgetting the modulus. That version does have two roots, minus 1 and minus 2, but both are negative and the modulus rules them out.
why_wrong.3: 4 would be the count if the modulus produced two quadratics each with two roots, but neither branch has real roots here.

why_correct: Let the roots be alpha and 2 alpha. Their sum is 3 alpha, which equals minus 2b over a, and their product is 2 alpha squared, which equals c over a. Eliminating alpha between the two gives 8b squared equal to 9ac.

why_wrong.0: 4b squared equal to ac has the wrong numerical factors. Both the 3 from the sum and the 2 from the product must survive into the final relation.
why_wrong.1: 4b squared equal to 3ac is the result of squaring only part of the substitution.
why_wrong.2: b squared equal to 9ac drops the factor from the doubled root in the product. A useful check is that the relation must reduce correctly when the two roots are equal, which is a separate condition.

why_correct: The first inequality gives x between minus 4 and 6. The second gives x at most minus 2 or at least 2. Both must hold, so the answer is the part of minus 4 to 6 that survives, namely minus 4 to minus 2 together with 2 to 6.

why_wrong.0: The symbol here is intersection, but those two intervals have no point in common, so the intersection would be empty. The two pieces are joined by union.
why_wrong.2: The empty set is wrong, since x equal to 3 satisfies both conditions.
why_wrong.3: Only the negative piece leaves out the whole of 2 to 6, which also satisfies both. The modulus condition on x alone splits into two branches, and both must be kept.

why_correct: The inequality says the modulus of x minus 4 is less than 2, which gives x between 2 and 6. Since x equal to 4 is excluded by the question, the solution is 2 to 4 together with 4 to 6.

why_wrong.0: The open interval from 2 to 6 forgets to remove 4, where the expression is undefined.
why_wrong.2: Extending to infinity is wrong. Large values of x make the fraction small, so the inequality fails there.
why_wrong.3: Extending to minus infinity is wrong for the same reason. Multiplying an inequality by a modulus is safe here because the modulus is positive, but the excluded point must still be removed.

why_correct: Writing both permutations as factorials, the ratio simplifies to n plus 5 times n plus 4, all over 4. Setting that equal to 11 times n minus 1 over 2 gives the quadratic n squared minus 13n plus 42 equal to 0, whose roots are 6 and 7. Of these, 6 is the option offered.

why_wrong.0: 5 does not satisfy the equation. Substituting it gives 90 over 4 on the left and 22 on the right.
why_wrong.2: 8 fails as well, since the quadratic factorises as n minus 6 times n minus 7.
why_wrong.3: 10 is far outside the solution set. Always simplify the permutation ratio to a small product before solving, rather than expanding the factorials.

why_correct: Every such number has four digits with the thousands digit 1, 2 or 3, giving 3 choices. Each of the other three digits may be any of the five, giving 5 cubed, that is 125. So the count is 3 times 125, which is 375.

why_wrong.0: 125 counts only one choice of leading digit instead of three.
why_wrong.1: 105 does not arise from any correct counting here and looks like an arithmetic slip.
why_wrong.3: 625 is 5 to the fourth, which would allow 0 and 4 as leading digits too. That would let in numbers below 1000 and at or above 4000, both excluded.

why_correct: If nCr equals nCs with r not equal to s, then r plus s equals n. Here 2 plus 3 gives n equal to 5, and 5C4 is 5.

why_wrong.0: 3 would be the answer if n were smaller, but the condition fixes n at 5.
why_wrong.1: 4 comes from confusing the answer with the lower index. 5C4 equals 5C1, which is 5.
why_wrong.3: 7 does not arise from any correct step. The identity to remember is nCr equals nC n minus r.

why_correct: The function is 1 for positive x and minus 1 for negative x. So f of x and f of minus x are always opposite in sign, their difference is plus or minus 2, and its modulus is 2.

why_wrong.0: 0 would require f to be an even function, taking the same value at x and minus x. This function is odd instead.
why_wrong.1: 1 is the value of the function itself for positive x, not of the difference.
why_wrong.2: Minus 1 cannot be right, since the question takes a modulus and a modulus is never negative.

why_correct: Approaching 0 from the right the expression is 1, and from the left it is minus 1. The one-sided limits differ, so the limit does not exist.

why_wrong.0: 0 would need the function to approach zero, but it only ever takes the values 1 and minus 1.
why_wrong.1: Minus 1 is the left-hand limit alone. A limit exists only if both sides agree.
why_wrong.2: 1 is the right-hand limit alone, and the same objection applies. Whenever a modulus sits over the variable at the point in question, check both sides separately.

why_correct: At x equal to 3 the expression is 0 over 0, so rationalise the numerator. Multiplying above and below by the sum of the roots gives x squared minus 9 over x minus 3 times the sum, which cancels to x plus 3 over the sum, and at x equal to 3 that is 6 over 2 root 19, or 3 over root 19.

why_wrong.0: 0 would be the answer only if the numerator vanished faster than the denominator, but here they vanish at the same rate.
why_wrong.1: 6 over root 19 forgets to halve when the two square roots in the denominator are added at x equal to 3. Each is root 19, so the sum is 2 root 19.
why_wrong.3: Root 19 over 6 is the correct answer turned upside down.
